title: Scaphoid fracture and avascular necrosis
text:
The most commonly fractured carpal bone, classically from a fall on an outstretched hand; tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is the key sign and initial radiographs are often normal.
Blood from the radial artery enters distally and flows retrograde, so a waist fracture can devascularise the proximal pole, leading to avascular necrosis, non-union and eventually scaphoid non-union advanced collapse (SNAC) arthritis of the wrist.

title: Lunate dislocation and Kienböck disease
text:
Perilunate and lunate dislocations follow high-energy hyperextension; the displaced lunate ('spilled teacup' on lateral X-ray) can compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.
Kienböck disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the lunate, associated with negative ulnar variance; progressive collapse causes pain, stiffness and carpal instability.

title: Hook of hamate fracture
text: Seen in golfers, batters and racquet players when the handle strikes the hypothenar eminence. The hook forms the lateral wall of Guyon's canal, so fractures may irritate the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (weak intrinsics) and can rupture flexor tendons to the little finger if non-union develops.

title: Humeral fractures and the nerves at risk
text:
Surgical neck fracture: axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery (deltoid paralysis, loss of sensation over the 'regimental badge' area).
Midshaft (spiral groove) fracture: radial nerve, causing wrist drop with preserved triceps.
Supracondylar fracture (children): brachial artery and median/anterior interosseous nerve; missed ischaemia can lead to Volkmann ischaemic contracture.
Medial epicondyle fracture: ulnar nerve.

title: Clavicle fracture
text: Usually fractures at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, where the curvature changes. Sternocleidomastoid elevates the medial fragment while the weight of the limb and pectoralis major pull the lateral fragment down and medially. The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus lie just beneath and are rarely injured by displaced fragments.

title: Distal radius fractures
text:
Colles fracture: dorsally displaced and angulated distal fragment ('dinner-fork' deformity), typically in osteoporotic bone after a fall on the outstretched hand. Smith fracture is the volar-displaced counterpart.
Complications include acute carpal tunnel syndrome, malunion, extensor pollicis longus rupture and complex regional pain syndrome.
Galeazzi fracture (distal-third radial shaft with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint) needs operative fixation.

title: Monteggia fracture and nightstick fracture
text:
Monteggia fracture-dislocation: proximal ulnar fracture with anterior dislocation of the radial head; the posterior interosseous nerve can be stretched, producing finger drop without wrist drop.
An isolated ulnar shaft fracture from warding off a blow is a 'nightstick' fracture.

title: Carpal tunnel syndrome and median nerve lesions
text:
Compression in the carpal tunnel (pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, amyloidosis, repetitive use) causes nocturnal paraesthesia of the lateral 3.5 digits, positive Tinel/Phalen tests and eventually thenar wasting with weak abductor pollicis brevis and opponens. Sensation over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the retinaculum.
A lesion at the elbow adds loss of flexion of the lateral fingers: the 'hand of benediction' on attempting a fist. Anterior interosseous nerve palsy abolishes the 'OK' sign pinch without sensory loss.

title: Cubital tunnel syndrome and ulnar claw hand
text:
The ulnar nerve is exposed behind the medial epicondyle (the 'funny bone') and is the second commonest entrapment neuropathy. Loss of interossei and medial lumbricals gives clawing of the ring and little fingers, positive Froment sign (flexor pollicis longus substitutes for adductor pollicis) and Wartenberg sign.
Ulnar paradox: a distal lesion (e.g. at Guyon's canal) produces MORE clawing than a proximal one, because flexor digitorum profundus to the medial digits is spared and pulls the fingers into flexion.

title: Radial nerve palsy (wrist drop)
text:
Compression in the axilla (crutches) or against the humerus ('Saturday night palsy', drunk sleeping with the arm over a chair) or a spiral-groove fracture paralyses the wrist and finger extensors. The patient cannot extend the wrist, and grip is weak because the finger flexors lose their mechanical advantage. Sensory loss is small, over the dorsal first web space.
An axillary lesion also paralyses triceps.

title: Axillary nerve injury
text: Injured by anterior shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture of the humerus. Deltoid (and teres minor) paralysis causes weak abduction beyond the first 15° and a flattened shoulder contour, with numbness over the lateral upper arm (regimental badge area). Always test sensation before and after reducing a dislocated shoulder.

title: Musculocutaneous nerve injury
text: Uncommon in isolation because it is protected in the axilla, but can be injured by stab wounds or during coracoid surgery, or compressed between biceps and brachialis by heavy lifting. Elbow flexion weakens (brachioradialis still helps), supination weakens, and sensation is lost along the lateral forearm (lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve).

title: Winged scapula
text: The long thoracic nerve runs superficially on serratus anterior and is injured during axillary node clearance, by heavy backpacks or by blows to the lateral chest. Serratus anterior paralysis lets the medial border of the scapula lift off the chest wall when pushing against a wall, and elevation of the arm above the horizontal is impaired because upward rotation of the scapula is lost.

title: Subacromial impingement and rotator cuff tear
text: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the coraco-acromial arch and is the rotator cuff tendon most often degenerated, impinged and torn. A painful arc between about 60° and 120° of abduction is typical of impingement; a full-thickness tear makes it hard to initiate abduction (positive drop-arm sign). The tendon has a relatively hypovascular 'critical zone' near its insertion on the greater tubercle, where calcific tendinitis also occurs.

title: Erb and Klumpke palsies
text:
Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6) follows forced separation of head and shoulder (shoulder dystocia, motorcycle falls): the arm hangs adducted, medially rotated, with the forearm pronated, the 'waiter's tip' posture.
Klumpke palsy (C8-T1) follows forced abduction of the arm (grabbing a branch while falling, breech delivery): claw hand with intrinsic muscle paralysis, sometimes with Horner syndrome if the T1 sympathetic outflow is avulsed.
Pancoast tumours at the lung apex invade the lower trunk and the sympathetic chain in the same way.

title: Flexor tendon injuries and tenosynovitis
text:
Lacerations in 'zone II' (no man's land, from the distal palmar crease to the middle phalanx), where both flexor tendons share a tight fibro-osseous sheath, historically had the worst outcome because of adhesions. Avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx (jersey finger) usually affects the ring finger.
Pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis (Kanavel signs) can spread from the little finger and thumb sheaths into the forearm (horseshoe abscess).

title: De Quervain tenosynovitis
text: Stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment over the radial styloid, common in new parents lifting infants. Pain over the radial styloid is reproduced by the Finkelstein manoeuvre (ulnar deviation with the thumb clasped in the fist).

title: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)
text: An overuse enthesopathy of the common extensor origin, chiefly extensor carpi radialis brevis, with angiofibroblastic degeneration rather than true inflammation. Pain over the lateral epicondyle is worsened by resisted wrist extension and gripping.

title: Pronator syndrome
text: The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres and can be compressed there, giving aching forearm pain and paraesthesia similar to carpal tunnel syndrome but WITH sensory loss over the thenar eminence (the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist) and without nocturnal symptoms.

title: Biceps tendon rupture
text: Rupture of the long head tendon, usually in older people with rotator cuff disease, produces a distal bulge (the 'Popeye' sign) with surprisingly little loss of strength. Distal tendon rupture at the radial tuberosity, typically in middle-aged men lifting heavy loads, causes marked weakness of supination and usually needs surgical repair.

title: Dupuytren contracture
text: Myofibroblastic proliferation in the palmar fascia forms nodules and cords that progressively flex the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, most often of the ring and little fingers. Associated with Northern European ancestry, diabetes, alcohol use, epilepsy medication and Ledderhose (plantar) and Peyronie (penile) disease.
